# Final project 2: São Paulo on foot, by bike and by public transport {#sec-m5-projeto-sp}

This page redoes the final project study (@sec-m5-projeto) for **São Paulo**, the largest network in the
package, and goes beyond public transport in two directions:

1. **The terrain.** São Paulo is not flat: between the Tietê valley and the ridge of Avenida Paulista there
   are about 100 metres of difference in elevation. On foot and by bike, the climb weighs. `r5r` takes the terrain into account
   when the network folder has a digital elevation model (`.tif`).
2. **Cyclist stress.** Not every street is rideable for everyone. `r5r` classifies each
   segment with a **Level of Traffic Stress** (LTS), from 1 (tolerable
   for children) to 4 (only for those who face heavy traffic), and restricts routes to the level the
   cyclist accepts.

The questions:

- **How much does cutting the bus routes with the least service reduce access to jobs, and who loses
  most?** (the same as in the final project)
- **How much does the terrain reduce access to jobs on foot and by bike?**
- **How much of bike access depends on accepting stressful streets?**

::: {.callout-important}
## The `r5r` blocks are not run when the site is built

As in the multimodal routing chapter (@sec-m4-r5r), the blocks that build the network and compute
the matrices require JDK 21, about 8 GB of memory for the JVM and the São Paulo data. They are
ready to run on your machine; the page's maps, tables and charts use the results that
this same code produced. The full calculation takes about 45 minutes.

`R/gerar_resultados_projeto_sp.R` runs, in order, every calculation block on this page
(those labelled `calc-`), and it is what produced the results.
:::

## The data

There are three sources:

- the São Paulo package from the final project (`sao_paulo.7z`, in the
  [`dados-modulo5` Release](https://github.com/Joaobazzo/curso-r-transportes/releases/tag/dados-modulo5)),
  extracted in `data_raw/projeto_final/sao_paulo/`: the OpenStreetMap network, the SPTrans GTFS and
  the `aopdata` grid;
- the **digital elevation model** from AWS terrain *tiles* (derived from SRTM and
  Copernicus), downloaded with `elevatr` in the terrain block, as in the raster data chapter;
- and nothing else: everything the page computes comes from these files.

The results go to `dados/projeto_final_sp/`, separate from those of the Fortaleza final project.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

pasta_sp <- "data_raw/projeto_final/sao_paulo"     # network, GTFS and aopdata from the package
saidas   <- "dados/projeto_final_sp"                # this page's results
dir.create(saidas, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

partida <- as.POSIXct("2026-05-13 07:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")   # a Wednesday

# the populated hexagons: population, jobs and income quintile
aop <- readRDS(file.path(pasta_sp, "aop_sao_paulo.rds")) |>
  dplyr::filter(P001 > 0) |>
  dplyr::select(id_hex, populacao = P001, empregos = T001, renda = R002)

# one origin and destination point at the centre of each hexagon
xy <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_centroid(sf::st_geometry(aop)))
pontos <- data.frame(id = aop$id_hex, lon = xy[, 1], lat = xy[, 2])

# the places in the examples
se     <- data.frame(id = "se", lon = -46.6340, lat = -23.5504)                # Praça da Sé
bairro <- data.frame(id = "cidade_tiradentes", lon = -46.4020, lat = -23.5830) # Cidade Tiradentes
batata <- data.frame(id = "largo_da_batata", lon = -46.6936, lat = -23.5668)   # Pinheiros

nrow(pontos)
```

The page's maps are of hexagons. To keep the file light, each map loads the grid
only once (`add_source()`) and draws several layers on top of it, switchable in the selector:

```{r}
#| label: funcoes-mapa
num <- function(x, d = 0) format(round(x, d), big.mark = ",", nsmall = d)

# map with the grid as a single data source, with only the columns requested in ...
mapa_hex <- function(dados, ...) {
  dados <- dplyr::select(dados, ...)
  mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = dados, height = "525px") |>
    mapgl::add_source(id = "hex", data = dados)
}

# one layer of the grid, coloured by a column
camada <- function(mapa, coluna, titulo, faixa, cores = c("#F6DCCB", "#2F6B9A", "#173A57"),
                   visivel = TRUE) {
  mapa |>
    mapgl::add_fill_layer(
      id = titulo, source = "hex",
      fill_color = mapgl::interpolate(column = coluna,
                                      values = seq(faixa[1], faixa[2], length.out = length(cores)),
                                      stops = cores),
      fill_opacity = 0.75, tooltip = coluna,
      visibility = if (visivel) "visible" else "none"
    ) |>
    mapgl::add_legend(titulo, values = round(faixa), colors = cores, layer_id = titulo, add = TRUE)
}

seletor <- function(mapa) {
  mapgl::add_layers_control(mapa, position = "top-right", collapsible = FALSE, mode = "single")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mapa-pop
grade <- aop |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

mapa_hex(grade, populacao, empregos) |>
  camada("populacao", "Population", range(grade$populacao),
         cores = c("#F7F6F2", "#E7A07A", "#7A1F0F")) |>
  camada("empregos", "Jobs", c(0, stats::quantile(grade$empregos, 0.99)),
         cores = c("#F7F6F2", "#7FA7C9", "#173A57"), visivel = FALSE) |>
  seletor()
```

There are `r num(nrow(aop))` hexagons with `r num(sum(aop$populacao))` residents. Jobs are
concentrated in the expanded centre; population, on the outskirts. The jobs scale stops at the
99th percentile, so that the few hexagons with tens of thousands of jobs do not wash out the rest.

## The terrain

The elevation model comes from `elevatr`, the same source as in the raster data chapter: AWS terrain
*tiles*, derived from SRTM and Copernicus. The study area is the populated hexagons,
with a 10 km margin, the same rule as the OpenStreetMap crop; that way the terrain covers the whole network.
At zoom 10, each cell is about 70 metres.

```{r}
#| label: calc-relevo
#| eval: false
pasta_relevo <- "dados/brutos/sao_paulo_relevo"     # the network with terrain: .pbf + .tif, no GTFS
dir.create(pasta_relevo, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# the study area: the populated hexagons with a 10 km margin
area <- aop |>
  sf::st_union() |>
  sf::st_buffer(dist = 10000) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326) |>
  sf::st_sf()

dem_raw <- elevatr::get_elev_raster(locations = area, z = 10, clip = "bbox")
relevo  <- terra::rast(dem_raw)
names(relevo) <- "altitude"

# r5r requires the .tif in degrees (EPSG:4326); elevatr already returns that system
terra::crs(relevo) <- "EPSG:4326"
terra::writeRaster(relevo, file.path(pasta_relevo, "relevo_sao_paulo.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
file.copy(file.path(pasta_sp, "sao_paulo.osm.pbf"), pasta_relevo, overwrite = TRUE)

# mean elevation and slope of each hexagon
declividade <- terra::terrain(relevo, v = "slope", unit = "degrees")

hexagonos <- aop |>
  sf::st_transform(4326) |>       # the same system as the raster
  terra::vect()                   # terra wants the polygons in its own format

altitude_hex    <- terra::extract(relevo, hexagonos, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
declividade_hex <- terra::extract(declividade, hexagonos, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)

relevo_hex <- data.frame(
  id_hex      = aop$id_hex,       # extract returns the rows in the order of the polygons
  altitude    = altitude_hex$altitude,
  declividade = declividade_hex$slope
)
saveRDS(relevo_hex, file.path(saidas, "relevo_hex.rds"))

# a light version of the terrain for the static map: about 280 m, with hillshading
leve <- terra::aggregate(relevo, fact = 4, fun = "mean")
inclinacao  <- terra::terrain(leve, "slope", unit = "radians")
orientacao  <- terra::terrain(leve, "aspect", unit = "radians")
sombra <- terra::shade(inclinacao, orientacao, angle = 40, direction = 315)
grade_relevo <- as.data.frame(c(leve, sombra), xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
names(grade_relevo) <- c("x", "y", "altitude", "sombra")
saveRDS(grade_relevo, file.path(saidas, "relevo_grade.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
relevo_hex   <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "relevo_hex.rds"))
grade_relevo <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "relevo_grade.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-relevo
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "Terrain of the São Paulo region (AWS Terrain Tiles via `elevatr`), with hillshading and the outline of the populated hexagons."
contorno <- aop |>
  sf::st_union() |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

ggplot(grade_relevo, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = altitude)) +
  geom_raster(aes(alpha = sombra), fill = "grey10") +
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.35, 0), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#2F6B9A", "#A9C4DA", "#F7F6F2", "#E7A07A", "#7A1F0F"),
                       name = "Elevation (m)") +
  geom_sf(data = contorno, inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = NA, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(xy[, 1]), ylim = range(xy[, 2])) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| label: mapa-relevo
grade <- grade |>
  dplyr::left_join(relevo_hex, by = "id_hex") |>
  dplyr::mutate(altitude = round(altitude), declividade = round(declividade, 1))

mapa_hex(grade, declividade, altitude) |>
  camada("declividade", "Mean slope (degrees)", c(0, stats::quantile(grade$declividade, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)),
         cores = c("#F7F6F2", "#E7A07A", "#7A1F0F")) |>
  camada("altitude", "Mean elevation (m)", range(grade$altitude, na.rm = TRUE),
         cores = c("#2F6B9A", "#F7F6F2", "#7A1F0F"), visivel = FALSE) |>
  seletor()
```

On the population-weighted average, each resident lives in a hexagon with a slope of
`r num(weighted.mean(grade$declividade, grade$populacao, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` degrees.
The steepest slopes are at the edges: the Cantareira range, to the north, and the hills of the far south and
far east, where much of the outskirts is.

## Public transport: the final project study

This is the multimodal routing chapter with São Paulo's data, as in step 2 of the
final project, in a single block: the network, the time matrix, the isochrone from Sé, the itinerary from
Cidade Tiradentes to Sé, the road loading, the scenario without the quarter of routes with the fewest
trips and the comparison.

```{r}
#| label: calc-transporte-publico
#| eval: false
options(java.parameters = "-Xmx8G")     # before the first use of r5r

rede <- r5r::build_network(data_path = pasta_sp)   # no .tif in the folder: no terrain

matriz_tp <- function(r) {
  r5r::travel_time_matrix(
    r, origins = pontos, destinations = pontos,
    mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = partida,
    time_window = 60, percentiles = 50, max_walk_time = 20, max_trip_duration = 90
  )
}
ttm <- matriz_tp(rede)

iso <- r5r::isochrone(rede, origins = se, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
                      departure_datetime = partida, cutoffs = c(15, 30, 45, 60),
                      time_window = 60, max_walk_time = 20)
saveRDS(iso, file.path(saidas, "isocronas_tp.rds"))

itinerario <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(rede, origins = bairro, destinations = se,
                                        mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = partida,
                                        max_walk_time = 20, shortest_path = FALSE)
saveRDS(itinerario, file.path(saidas, "itinerario_tp.rds"))

# loading: from the 30 most populous hexagons to the 10 with the most jobs, by car
origens <- aop |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::slice_max(populacao, n = 30, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::select(origem = id_hex, populacao)

destinos <- aop |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::slice_max(empregos, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::select(destino = id_hex, empregos)

# every origin–destination pair, with a hypothetical flow: the origin's population split
# among the destinations, in proportion to each one's jobs
pares_od <- expand.grid(origem = origens$origem, destino = destinos$destino,
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(origem != destino) |>
  dplyr::left_join(origens, by = "origem") |>
  dplyr::left_join(destinos, by = "destino") |>
  dplyr::mutate(fluxo = populacao * empregos / sum(destinos$empregos))

rotas_carro <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(
  rede,
  origins      = pontos[match(pares_od$origem, pontos$id), ],
  destinations = pontos[match(pares_od$destino, pontos$id), ],
  mode = "CAR", departure_datetime = partida, shortest_path = TRUE
)

# each route gets its pair's flow; overline adds the flows up segment by segment
fluxos <- dplyr::select(pares_od, origem, destino, fluxo)
rotas_carro <- rotas_carro |>
  dplyr::left_join(fluxos, by = c("from_id" = "origem", "to_id" = "destino"))

carga <- stplanr::overline(rotas_carro, attrib = "fluxo")
saveRDS(carga, file.path(saidas, "carga.rds"))

# the scenario: without the quarter of routes with the fewest trips
gtfs <- gtfstools::read_gtfs(file.path(pasta_sp, "gtfs_sao_paulo.zip"))
viagens  <- dplyr::count(gtfs$trips, route_id, name = "viagens")
cortadas <- viagens$route_id[viagens$viagens <= stats::quantile(viagens$viagens, 0.25)]
saveRDS(cortadas, file.path(saidas, "linhas_cortadas.rds"))

gtfs_cenario <- gtfstools::filter_by_route_id(gtfs, route_id = cortadas, keep = FALSE)

pasta_cenario <- "dados/brutos/sao_paulo_cenario"
dir.create(pasta_cenario, showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(file.path(pasta_sp, "sao_paulo.osm.pbf"), pasta_cenario, overwrite = TRUE)
gtfstools::write_gtfs(gtfs_cenario, file.path(pasta_cenario, "gtfs_cenario.zip"))
unlink(file.path(pasta_cenario, "network.dat"))     # forces a rebuild with the new GTFS

r5r::stop_r5(rede)
rede_cenario <- r5r::build_network(data_path = pasta_cenario)
ttm_cenario  <- matriz_tp(rede_cenario)
r5r::stop_r5(rede_cenario)

uso_solo <- aop |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::rename(id = id_hex)

acesso_cum <- function(m, minutos) {
  accessibility::cumulative_cutoff(travel_matrix = m, land_use_data = uso_solo,
                                   opportunity = "empregos", travel_cost = "travel_time_p50",
                                   cutoff = minutos)
}

# jobs within 60 minutes, today and in the scenario, each in its own column
acesso_atual   <- acesso_cum(ttm, 60) |> dplyr::rename(atual = empregos)
acesso_cenario <- acesso_cum(ttm_cenario, 60) |> dplyr::rename(cenario = empregos)
moradores      <- dplyr::select(uso_solo, id, populacao, renda)

comparacao_tp <- acesso_atual |>
  dplyr::left_join(acesso_cenario, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::left_join(moradores, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(perda_abs = cenario - atual,
                perda_pct = dplyr::if_else(atual > 0, 100 * (cenario / atual - 1), NA_real_))
saveRDS(comparacao_tp, file.path(saidas, "comparacao_tp.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
iso_tp        <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "isocronas_tp.rds"))
itinerario_tp <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "itinerario_tp.rds"))
carga         <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "carga.rds"))
cortadas      <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "linhas_cortadas.rds"))
comparacao_tp <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "comparacao_tp.rds"))
```

### How far you get from Sé, and how you get there from Cidade Tiradentes

```{r}
#| label: mapa-isocrona-tp
iso_tp <- dplyr::arrange(iso_tp, dplyr::desc(isochrone))      # the smaller bands on top
cores_iso <- c("#173A57", "#2F6B9A", "#A9C4DA", "#F6DCCB")

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = iso_tp, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_fill_layer(id = "isocronas", source = iso_tp,
                        fill_color = mapgl::match_expr("isochrone", values = c(15, 30, 45, 60),
                                                       stops = cores_iso),
                        fill_opacity = 0.6, tooltip = "isochrone") |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Minutes from Sé", values = c(15, 30, 45, 60), colors = cores_iso,
                    type = "categorical")
```

```{r}
#| label: mapa-itinerario-tp
opcao <- dplyr::filter(itinerario_tp, option == 1)
modos <- unique(opcao$mode)
cores_modo <- c(WALK = "#7A7A7A", BUS = "#2F6B9A", RAIL = "#C2542D", SUBWAY = "#7A1F0F",
                TRAM = "#E7A07A")[modos]

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = opcao, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "itinerario", source = opcao,
                        line_color = mapgl::match_expr("mode", values = modos,
                                                       stops = unname(cores_modo)),
                        line_width = 5, tooltip = "route") |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Mode", values = modos, colors = unname(cores_modo), type = "categorical")
```

The fastest trip from Cidade Tiradentes to Sé takes `r round(opcao$total_duration[1])` minutes,
combining `r paste(setdiff(unique(opcao$route), ""), collapse = ", ")`. In São Paulo, unlike
the other cities in the package, the SPTrans GTFS includes the metro and the CPTM trains, and it is
through them that the long trips from the eastern outskirts go.

### The scenario: who loses access with the cut

```{r}
#| label: mapa-cenario-tp
resultado_tp <- dplyr::select(comparacao_tp, id_hex = id, atual, cenario, perda_abs)
grade <- dplyr::left_join(grade, resultado_tp, by = "id_hex")

faixa_tp <- c(0, max(grade$atual, na.rm = TRUE))
limite   <- max(abs(grade$perda_abs), na.rm = TRUE)

mapa_hex(grade, atual, cenario, perda_abs) |>
  camada("atual", "Jobs within 60 min: today", faixa_tp) |>
  camada("cenario", "Jobs within 60 min: scenario", faixa_tp, visivel = FALSE) |>
  camada("perda_abs", "Change with the cut", c(-limite, limite),
         cores = c("#C2542D", "#F7F6F2", "#2F6B9A"), visivel = FALSE) |>
  seletor()
```

The scenario removes `r length(cortadas)` routes. The average change for each income quintile,
weighted by population (1 = the poorest 20%):

```{r}
#| label: tab-renda-tp
por_renda_tp <- comparacao_tp |>
  dplyr::filter(renda %in% 1:5) |>
  dplyr::summarise(pessoas = sum(populacao),
                   atual = weighted.mean(as.numeric(atual), populacao, na.rm = TRUE),   # integers would overflow
                   variacao_pct = weighted.mean(perda_pct, populacao, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .by = renda) |>
  dplyr::arrange(renda)

knitr::kable(por_renda_tp, digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Income quintile", "People", "Jobs within 60 min (mean)",
                           "Change with the cut (%)"))
```

The poorest reach far fewer jobs today and lose a bigger share with the cut: the routes
with the least service are, to a large extent, those that feed the distant neighbourhoods.

carga <- carga |>

## On foot and by bike, with and without terrain

To measure the effect of terrain, the same matrix is computed on two networks:

- the **flat** one, the package's, with no `.tif` in the folder;
- the one **with terrain**, a folder with the same `.pbf` and the `.tif` from the previous block. With the `.tif` there,
  `build_network()` uses Tobler's function (`elevation = "TOBLER"`, the default), which reduces
  speed on climbs and increases it slightly on gentle descents, on foot and by bike.

The indicator is the number of jobs reachable within **30 minutes**, at 3.6 km/h on foot and
12 km/h by bike. For the bike, `r5r`'s default stress level applies, `max_lts = 2`: the
ordinary cyclist, who only rides on cycle paths, cycle lanes and quiet streets (the next section varies
this level).

The block has four steps: two functions that repeat, the two measures on the flat network, the two on the
network with terrain and, at the end, the four measures in a single table.

```{r}
#| label: calc-ativo
#| eval: false
pasta_relevo <- "dados/brutos/sao_paulo_relevo"

# ---- 1. The block's two functions ------------------------------------

# travel time matrix on foot or by bike, from every hexagon to every other.
# max_trip_duration = 30: longer trips do not even enter the matrix.
# lts: the maximum stress level the cyclist accepts (r5r ignores it on foot)
matriz_ativa <- function(rede, modo, lts = 2) {
  r5r::travel_time_matrix(
    rede, origins = pontos, destinations = pontos, mode = modo,
    departure_datetime = partida, max_trip_duration = 30,
    walk_speed = 3.6, bike_speed = 12, max_lts = lts
  )
}

# jobs reachable within 30 minutes from each hexagon.
# Returns a table with two columns: id (the hexagon) and empregos (jobs)
acesso_30 <- function(matriz) {
  accessibility::cumulative_cutoff(travel_matrix = matriz, land_use_data = uso_solo,
                                   opportunity = "empregos", travel_cost = "travel_time_p50",
                                   cutoff = 30)
}

# ---- 2. Flat network (the package's, already built in the public transport block) ----
rede_plana <- r5r::build_network(data_path = pasta_sp)

# each measure gets the name of its mode and network combination, so they do not get mixed up later
a_pe_plano <- matriz_ativa(rede_plana, "WALK") |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(a_pe_plano = empregos)

bici_plano <- matriz_ativa(rede_plana, "BICYCLE") |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(bici_plano = empregos)

# the bike route from Largo da Batata to Sé, for the next subsection
rota_plana <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(rede_plana, origins = batata, destinations = se,
                                        mode = "BICYCLE", bike_speed = 12, max_lts = 2,
                                        departure_datetime = partida)
r5r::stop_r5(rede_plana)

# ---- 3. Network with terrain: the same measures ----------------------
# overwrite = TRUE rebuilds the network if the .tif changes
rede_relevo <- r5r::build_network(data_path = pasta_relevo, elevation = "TOBLER",
                                  overwrite = TRUE)

a_pe_relevo <- matriz_ativa(rede_relevo, "WALK") |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(a_pe_relevo = empregos)

bici_relevo <- matriz_ativa(rede_relevo, "BICYCLE") |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(bici_relevo = empregos)

rota_relevo <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(rede_relevo, origins = batata, destinations = se,
                                         mode = "BICYCLE", bike_speed = 12, max_lts = 2,
                                         departure_datetime = partida)
# rede_relevo stays open: the following blocks use it

# ---- 4. The four measures in a single table, one row per hexagon ----
# full_join: if a hexagon is missing from one of the tables, it stays, with NA in that table's column
ativo <- a_pe_plano |>
  dplyr::full_join(bici_plano,  by = "id") |>
  dplyr::full_join(a_pe_relevo, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::full_join(bici_relevo, by = "id")

saveRDS(ativo, file.path(saidas, "acesso_ativo.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ativo <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "acesso_ativo.rds"))
```

The `ativo` table has one row per hexagon and one column for each measure. To take the city
average, each hexagon must be weighted by its number of residents: a hexagon with 5,000 people counts
more than one with 50. So the first step is to bring in the population:

```{r}
#| label: tab-ativo
# 1. the population and income of each hexagon, without the geometry
moradores <- aop |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::select(id = id_hex, populacao, renda)

# 2. join with the access measures. A hexagon with no result (NA) reaches
#    no job within 30 minutes: it becomes 0
ativo_pop <- ativo |>
  dplyr::left_join(moradores, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    a_pe_plano  = dplyr::coalesce(a_pe_plano, 0),
    bici_plano  = dplyr::coalesce(bici_plano, 0),
    a_pe_relevo = dplyr::coalesce(a_pe_relevo, 0),
    bici_relevo = dplyr::coalesce(bici_relevo, 0)
  )

# 3. the mean of each measure, weighted by population
medias <- ativo_pop |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    a_pe_plano  = weighted.mean(a_pe_plano, populacao),
    bici_plano  = weighted.mean(bici_plano, populacao),
    a_pe_relevo = weighted.mean(a_pe_relevo, populacao),
    bici_relevo = weighted.mean(bici_relevo, populacao)
  )

# 4. the table for the reader: one row per mode, without and with terrain
resumo_ativo <- data.frame(
  modo   = c("On foot", "Bike (LTS 2)"),
  plano  = c(medias$a_pe_plano, medias$bici_plano),
  relevo = c(medias$a_pe_relevo, medias$bici_relevo)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(variacao = 100 * (relevo / plano - 1))

knitr::kable(resumo_ativo, digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Mode", "Without terrain", "With terrain", "Change (%)"),
             caption = "Jobs reachable within 30 minutes, population-weighted mean")
```

Terrain reduces access on foot by `r num(abs(resumo_ativo$variacao[1]), 1)`% and by bike by
`r num(abs(resumo_ativo$variacao[2]), 1)`%, on the population average. The average effect hides the
geography: where it weighs is on the slopes. The map shows the change for each hexagon by bike:

```{r}
#| label: mapa-ativo
# the measures that go on the map, with the grid's column name (id_hex)
medidas_mapa <- dplyr::select(ativo_pop, id_hex = id, bici_plano, bici_relevo, a_pe_relevo)

# the change for each hexagon by bike, in %. With no access on the flat network, the calculation does not exist
grade <- grade |>
  dplyr::left_join(medidas_mapa, by = "id_hex") |>
  dplyr::mutate(var_relevo = dplyr::if_else(bici_plano > 0,
                                            round(100 * (bici_relevo / bici_plano - 1), 1),
                                            NA_real_))

# the access scale stops at the 99th percentile, as in the jobs map
faixa_bici <- c(0, stats::quantile(grade$bici_plano, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))
faixa_a_pe <- c(0, stats::quantile(grade$a_pe_relevo, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))

mapa_hex(grade, var_relevo, bici_plano, bici_relevo, a_pe_relevo) |>
  camada("var_relevo", "Effect of terrain on cycling (%)", c(-50, 50),
         cores = c("#C2542D", "#F7F6F2", "#2F6B9A")) |>
  camada("bici_plano", "Bike, without terrain", faixa_bici, visivel = FALSE) |>
  camada("bici_relevo", "Bike, with terrain", faixa_bici, visivel = FALSE) |>
  camada("a_pe_relevo", "On foot, with terrain", faixa_a_pe, visivel = FALSE) |>
  seletor()
```

The change scale runs from −50% to +50%; the effect is almost entirely negative. Bluish hexagons are
those that sit high up and go down to the jobs: the gentle descent speeds the bike up.

### A route over the ridge

The city average says how much the terrain weighs, but it does not show **how**. For that, it is worth looking at a
single trip. From Largo da Batata, in Pinheiros, to Praça da Sé, the bike has to climb the Paulista
ridge and go down to the Anhangabaú valley. With terrain, `r5r` estimates a longer time and
may choose another path, one that climbs less.

The two routes were already computed in the previous block (`rota_plana` and `rota_relevo`). To
compare them, we still need the **elevation profile** of each one: the elevation along the path, read from the
same `.tif` used by the network. The function below does this in five steps:

```{r}
#| label: calc-perfil
#| eval: false
perfil_rota <- function(rota) {
  # 1. the route's legs, in the order of the trip
  rota <- rota[order(rota$segment), ]

  # 2. the coordinates of every vertex, in a matrix (X and Y columns),
  #    and with them a single line, from the start to the end of the trip
  vertices <- sf::st_coordinates(rota)[, c("X", "Y")]
  linha <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(vertices), crs = 4326)

  # 3. one point every 25 m along the line; to measure in metres, the line goes
  #    to SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 23S
  linha_m  <- sf::st_transform(linha, 31983)
  pontos_m <- sf::st_line_sample(linha_m, density = 1 / 25) |>
    sf::st_cast("POINT")

  # 4. the distance travelled up to each point: the sum of the steps between neighbouring points
  passos <- sf::st_distance(pontos_m[-length(pontos_m)], pontos_m[-1], by_element = TRUE)
  distancia_km <- c(0, cumsum(as.numeric(passos))) / 1000

  # 5. the elevation of each point, read from the .tif (which is in degrees)
  mde <- terra::rast(file.path(pasta_relevo, "relevo_sao_paulo.tif"))
  pontos_graus <- terra::vect(sf::st_transform(pontos_m, 4326))
  altitude <- terra::extract(mde, pontos_graus)$altitude

  data.frame(distancia = distancia_km, altitude = altitude)
}
```

With the function ready, it remains to apply it to the routes. A third route joins the comparison: that of the
cyclist who accepts **any street**, including avenues with heavy traffic (`max_lts = 4`).
It anticipates the next section, on traffic stress.

```{r}
#| label: calc-rotas
#| eval: false
# the third route: on the network with terrain, with no stress restriction
rota_lts4 <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(rede_relevo, origins = batata, destinations = se,
                                       mode = "BICYCLE", bike_speed = 12, max_lts = 4,
                                       departure_datetime = partida)

# the three routes in a single table, with a column that says which is which
rotas_bici <- rbind(
  dplyr::mutate(rota_plana,  rede = "Flat, LTS 2"),
  dplyr::mutate(rota_relevo, rede = "Terrain, LTS 2"),
  dplyr::mutate(rota_lts4,   rede = "Terrain, LTS 4")
)
saveRDS(rotas_bici, file.path(saidas, "rotas_bici.rds"))

# the profile of each route, one at a time, then the three stacked
perfis <- list()
for (nome in unique(rotas_bici$rede)) {
  rota   <- rotas_bici[rotas_bici$rede == nome, ]
  perfil <- perfil_rota(rota)
  perfis[[nome]] <- data.frame(rede = nome, perfil)
}
perfis <- dplyr::bind_rows(perfis)
saveRDS(perfis, file.path(saidas, "perfis_bici.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rotas_bici <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "rotas_bici.rds"))
perfis     <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "perfis_bici.rds"))

# the saved results come from the Portuguese version of this page: translate the labels
rotulos <- c("Sem relevo, LTS 2" = "Flat, LTS 2",
             "Com relevo, LTS 2" = "Terrain, LTS 2",
             "Com relevo, LTS 4" = "Terrain, LTS 4")
traduzir <- function(x) dplyr::coalesce(unname(rotulos[x]), x)
rotas_bici$rede <- traduzir(rotas_bici$rede)
perfis$rede     <- traduzir(perfis$rede)
```

First, the path. On the map, the two routes of the ordinary cyclist (LTS 2), without and with terrain:

```{r}
#| label: mapa-rotas-relevo
duas <- rotas_bici |>
  dplyr::filter(rede != "Terrain, LTS 4") |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)
cores_rota <- c("Flat, LTS 2" = "#7A7A7A", "Terrain, LTS 2" = "#C2542D")

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = duas, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "rotas", source = duas,
                        line_color = mapgl::match_expr("rede", values = names(cores_rota),
                                                       stops = unname(cores_rota)),
                        line_width = 5, line_opacity = 0.8, tooltip = "total_duration") |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Bike route", values = names(cores_rota),
                    colors = unname(cores_rota), type = "categorical")
```

Then, the terrain along each path. The profile shows where the climbs are:

```{r}
#| label: fig-perfil
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Elevation profile of the bike routes from Largo da Batata to Praça da Sé."
ggplot(perfis, aes(distancia, altitude, colour = rede)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(cores_rota, "Terrain, LTS 4" = "#2F6B9A"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Distance travelled (km)", y = "Elevation (m)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Finally, the numbers for each route. Time and distance come from `r5r`; the cumulative climb is the
sum of every stretch in which the profile goes up:

```{r}
#| label: tab-rotas
# time and distance: r5r repeats the trip total on each leg, one value per route is enough
tempo_rotas <- rotas_bici |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(minutos = max(total_duration), km = max(total_distance) / 1000, .by = rede)

# cumulative climb: the positive elevation differences between neighbouring points of the profile
subida_rotas <- perfis |>
  dplyr::summarise(subida = sum(pmax(diff(altitude), 0), na.rm = TRUE), .by = rede)

tab_rotas <- dplyr::left_join(tempo_rotas, subida_rotas, by = "rede")

knitr::kable(tab_rotas, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Route", "Time (min)", "Distance (km)", "Cumulative climb (m)"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rota_tab <- function(nome) tab_rotas[tab_rotas$rede == nome, ]
plana_2  <- rota_tab("Flat, LTS 2")
relevo_2 <- rota_tab("Terrain, LTS 2")
relevo_4 <- rota_tab("Terrain, LTS 4")
```

With terrain, the same trip goes from `r num(plana_2$minutos, 1)` to
`r num(relevo_2$minutos, 1)` minutes: `r5r` slows the bike down on climbs. The cyclist
who accepts any street, on the other hand, arrives in `r num(relevo_4$minutos, 1)` minutes, by a shorter path
(`r num(relevo_4$km, 1)` km) with less climbing (`r num(relevo_4$subida)` m): the avenues,
out of the ordinary cyclist's reach, shorten the trip. How much this weighs on the whole city's access
is the subject of the next section.

## Cycling and traffic stress

`r5r` assigns each street segment a stress level from OpenStreetMap
tags: road type, number of lanes, speed and the presence of a cycle path or cycle lane.
With `max_lts = 2`, the route only uses level 1 and 2 segments; on the others, the cyclist gets off and pushes the
bike, at walking speed.

The block below uses the network with terrain, still open, for three things: access to jobs with
each tolerated stress level, the length of streets at each level and the streets in the corridor between
Pinheiros and Sé, for the map.

```{r}
#| label: calc-lts
#| eval: false
# ---- 1. Access with each tolerated stress level ----------------------
# LTS 2 was already computed in the bike-with-terrain block: only the column name changes
lts2 <- dplyr::rename(bici_relevo, lts2 = bici_relevo)

# the other three levels: one matrix for each
lts1 <- matriz_ativa(rede_relevo, "BICYCLE", lts = 1) |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(lts1 = empregos)

lts3 <- matriz_ativa(rede_relevo, "BICYCLE", lts = 3) |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(lts3 = empregos)

lts4 <- matriz_ativa(rede_relevo, "BICYCLE", lts = 4) |>
  acesso_30() |>
  dplyr::rename(lts4 = empregos)

# the four in a single table, one row per hexagon
acesso_lts <- lts1 |>
  dplyr::full_join(lts2, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::full_join(lts3, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::full_join(lts4, by = "id")
saveRDS(acesso_lts, file.path(saidas, "acesso_lts.rds"))

# ---- 2. The stress level of each rideable street segment -------------
ruas <- r5r::street_network_to_sf(rede_relevo)$edges |>
  dplyr::filter(bicycle) |>
  # the network has one record per direction of each segment: keep just one
  dplyr::mutate(par = paste(pmin(from_vertex, to_vertex), pmax(from_vertex, to_vertex))) |>
  dplyr::filter(!duplicated(par))

km_lts <- ruas |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(km = sum(length) / 1000, .by = bicycle_lts) |>
  dplyr::arrange(bicycle_lts)
saveRDS(km_lts, file.path(saidas, "km_lts.rds"))

# ---- 3. For the map: the streets in a 1.5 km corridor around the Pinheiros–Sé line ----
corredor <- rbind(batata, se) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_union() |>
  sf::st_cast("LINESTRING") |>
  sf::st_transform(31983) |>           # for the buffer in metres
  sf::st_buffer(1500) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

ruas_corredor <- ruas |>
  sf::st_filter(corredor) |>           # only the streets touching the corridor
  dplyr::select(osm_id, street_class, bicycle_lts)
saveRDS(ruas_corredor, file.path(saidas, "ruas_corredor.rds"))

r5r::stop_r5(rede_relevo)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
acesso_lts    <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "acesso_lts.rds"))
km_lts        <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "km_lts.rds"))
ruas_corredor <- readRDS(file.path(saidas, "ruas_corredor.rds"))
```

The length of rideable streets at each level, across the whole OpenStreetMap crop (the city and
part of the neighbouring municipalities):

```{r}
#| label: tab-km-lts
km_lts |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct = 100 * km / sum(km)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
               col.names = c("Stress level (LTS)", "Length (km)", "% of the rideable network"))
```

In the corridor between Pinheiros and Sé, the LTS 4 avenues form the main grid, and the
cycle paths and quiet streets appear as disconnected stretches between them:

```{r}
#| label: mapa-lts
cores_lts <- c("#2F6B9A", "#7FA7C9", "#E7A07A", "#7A1F0F")

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = ruas_corredor,
                height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "lts", source = ruas_corredor,
                        line_color = mapgl::match_expr("bicycle_lts", values = 1:4,
                                                       stops = cores_lts),
                        line_width = 2, tooltip = "street_class") |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Stress level (LTS)", values = 1:4, colors = cores_lts,
                    type = "categorical")
```

How much of bike access depends on accepting more stressful streets? The jobs reachable
within 30 minutes, on the network with terrain, for each maximum tolerated level. The route is the same as for the terrain
table: bring in the population, replace missing results with zero and take the weighted mean,
now by income quintile:

```{r}
#| label: tab-lts-renda
# 1. bring in population and income (the moradores table, from the on-foot and bike table)
lts_pop <- acesso_lts |>
  dplyr::left_join(moradores, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    lts1 = dplyr::coalesce(lts1, 0),
    lts2 = dplyr::coalesce(lts2, 0),
    lts3 = dplyr::coalesce(lts3, 0),
    lts4 = dplyr::coalesce(lts4, 0)
  )

# 2. the weighted mean of each level, by income quintile
por_renda_lts <- lts_pop |>
  dplyr::filter(renda %in% 1:5) |>               # aopdata has a few hexagons with quintile 0
  dplyr::summarise(
    lts1 = weighted.mean(lts1, populacao),
    lts2 = weighted.mean(lts2, populacao),
    lts3 = weighted.mean(lts3, populacao),
    lts4 = weighted.mean(lts4, populacao),
    .by = renda
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(renda)

# 3. how much of the "any street" access (LTS 4) the ordinary cyclist (LTS 2) keeps
por_renda_lts <- por_renda_lts |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct_lts2 = 100 * lts2 / lts4)

knitr::kable(por_renda_lts, digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Income quintile", "LTS 1", "LTS 2", "LTS 3", "LTS 4",
                           "LTS 2 / LTS 4 (%)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lts
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Jobs reachable by bike within 30 minutes, by tolerated stress level and income quintile (population-weighted mean)."
# for the chart, one row per quintile and level
por_renda_lts_longa <- por_renda_lts |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(lts1:lts4, names_to = "lts", values_to = "empregos") |>
  dplyr::mutate(lts = sub("lts", "LTS ", lts))

ggplot(por_renda_lts_longa, aes(factor(renda), empregos, fill = lts)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cores_lts, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = "Income quintile (1 = poorest)", y = "Jobs within 30 min by bike") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}

# the measures that go on the map, with the grid's column name (id_hex)
lts_mapa <- dplyr::select(lts_pop, id_hex = id, lts1, lts2, lts4)

grade <- grade |>
  dplyr::left_join(lts_mapa, by = "id_hex") |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct_lts2 = dplyr::if_else(lts4 > 0, round(100 * lts2 / lts4), NA_real_))

faixa_lts <- c(0, stats::quantile(grade$lts4, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))

mapa_hex(grade, pct_lts2, lts1, lts2, lts4) |>
  camada("pct_lts2", "Access with LTS 2, as % of LTS 4", c(0, 100),
         cores = c("#7A1F0F", "#E7A07A", "#F7F6F2")) |>
  camada("lts1", "Bike, LTS 1", faixa_lts, visivel = FALSE) |>
  camada("lts2", "Bike, LTS 2", faixa_lts, visivel = FALSE) |>
  camada("lts4", "Bike, LTS 4", faixa_lts, visivel = FALSE) |>
  seletor()
```

```{r}
#| label: mapa-rotas-lts
duas_lts <- rotas_bici |>
  dplyr::filter(rede != "Flat, LTS 2") |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)
cores_rota_lts <- c("Terrain, LTS 2" = "#C2542D", "Terrain, LTS 4" = "#2F6B9A")

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = duas_lts, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(id = "rotas_lts", source = duas_lts,
                        line_color = mapgl::match_expr("rede", values = names(cores_rota_lts),
                                                       stops = unname(cores_rota_lts)),
                        line_width = 5, line_opacity = 0.8, tooltip = "total_duration") |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Bike route", values = names(cores_rota_lts),
                    colors = unname(cores_rota_lts), type = "categorical")
```

With LTS 2, the average resident reaches
`r num(weighted.mean(lts_pop$lts2, lts_pop$populacao))` jobs within 30 minutes by bike;
accepting any street (LTS 4), `r num(weighted.mean(lts_pop$lts4, lts_pop$populacao))`. The
difference is the size of the problem a continuous cycle network would solve: the jobs that
are within reach of the bike, but only for those who face the traffic.

## Conclusions

(What the results show about each question, who is most affected and what this implies for
public transport, pavement and cycle path policy.)

## Limitations

- The SPTrans GTFS was converted from frequencies to fixed times only between 5:00 and 11:00; the
  result holds for the morning peak.
- `elevatr`'s *tiles* are good for exploratory analysis, but they mix sources (SRTM,
  Copernicus) and, in dense areas, part of the buildings and trees gets into the elevation. For an official
  study, prefer a citable source, such as TOPODATA/INPE.
- Tobler's function was estimated for walking; R5 also applies it to cycling. E-bikes,
  increasingly common, hardly feel the terrain.
- The stress level comes from OpenStreetMap tags: an unmapped cycle path, or a street
  without the number of lanes and speed, may fall into the wrong level.
- Population, jobs and income are from 2019 (`aopdata`); the transport network is from 2026.
- The loading considers only cars and a small set of origin–destination pairs, with
  hypothetical flows.
